conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes 'No' to the question of whether ginkgo extract relieves tinnitus symptoms, citing Cochrane systematic reviews that show no meaningful benefit and clinical guidelines recommending against its use.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: No—current evidence does not reliably show that ginkgo extract relieves tinnitus symptoms.**

The best evidence is a Cochrane systematic review of randomized controlled trials comparing ginkgo with placebo, no treatment, or education. The review does not establish a meaningful benefit for tinnitus; the available studies are limited and uncertainty remains. Its safety evidence was also low-certainty: across four studies (1,154 participants), ginkgo produced little or no difference in bleeding or seizures, but that does not prove it is risk-free.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013514_ginkgo-biloba-herbal-supplement-tinnitus

An earlier Cochrane review likewise concluded that limited evidence did **not** demonstrate effectiveness when tinnitus was the primary complaint.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23543524/

This interpretation is reflected in the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery guideline: it recommends clinicians **not** use ginkgo biloba (or other dietary supplements) for persistent, bothersome tinnitus.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25273878/

Safety matters: ginkgo can interact with medicines and may increase bleeding risk, particularly with anticoagulants such as warfarin. Do not start it for tinnitus without checking with a clinician or pharmacist if you take any regular medication.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginkgo
